title: Maximum of three
instructorPromptText: Write a function that takes three numbers and returns the largest one. Do not use the built-in max() function.

specGateDimensions.description: What should the function return when two or all three inputs are equal (e.g., max_of_three(5, 5, 3))?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Ties have an obvious answer (return the tied value) but force the student to notice that their comparison operators — < vs <= — don't actually matter for correctness here, which is a useful observation.

specGateDimensions.description: Does the function need to handle floats, negative numbers, and mixed int/float inputs, or only positive integers?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Students often implicitly assume positive integers and write code that happens to work for negatives anyway; committing to the contract clarifies what the tests should cover.

specGateDimensions.description: Will you compare the three numbers with a chain of if/elif branches, or reduce pairwise (find max of first two, then compare to third)?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Both strategies are valid and the student must commit to one before coding, since mixing them mid-implementation is a common source of tangled logic.

expectedDivergences.pattern: Student writes `if a > b and a > c` / `elif b > a and b > c` but omits the final `else` or a third branch, so certain tie configurations fall through and return None
Student uses `if a > b > c` thinking it checks 'a is the largest', misunderstanding Python's chained comparison semantics
Spec commits to handling negatives but code initializes a running maximum to 0 instead of to one of the inputs, causing wrong answers on all-negative inputs
Plan describes three if/elif branches; code uses a running-maximum accumulator pattern (`m = a; if b > m: m = b; if c > m: m = c`) — coherent simplification
Student sorts a list of the three values and returns the last element — satisfies the spec and avoids max() but sidesteps the comparison logic the exercise is meant to teach
